items.title: One short form, two long choices
items.caption: Both long forms are printed for every verb here. The equals sign keeps the join visible in this book; ordinary writing joins the parts without it.

items.title: The ending has two possible homes

states.label: On the verb
states.sm: ʻO ai na faʻatau=a mai le tusi?
states.note: The long-form ending is on the verb.

states.label: On the direction word
states.sm: ʻO ai na faʻatau mai=a le tusi?
states.note: The ending sits on the following direction word instead. Both positions are accepted.

items.caption: The ending moves; the meaning stays the same. Both printed forms ask the same question.

items.title: Which rule settles the shape?

options.label: A command requires the short form
The choice is open outside the command rules

prompts.why: A command to do something takes the short form.

prompts.sm: ʻAua le tatala=ina le pusa lenā.
prompts.why: Forbidding with *ʻaua le* requires the long form.

prompts.sm: Sā faitau e le teine le vāega.
prompts.why: This plain report uses the short form as the default. Outside the two command positions, the chapter gives tendencies rather than a fixed rule.

items.intro: Read the printed sentence and decide whether a command rule fixes the verb form.
